t: Digital Skills: Google Classroom and the Cloud
l: Hello and welcome to Mr Butler's Digital Technology podcast. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. This episode is all about digital skills: Google Classroom and the cloud.
If you've just started secondary school, this is the stuff you'll use every single week. Joining classes, handing in homework, sharing documents, and not losing your work.

We'll cover what the cloud is, Google Classroom, assignments, Google Drive, Docs, Slides and Sheets, sharing, working together, uploading files, staying organised, being a good digital citizen, and fixing common problems.
That's a lot. Let's get going. Conor, what actually is the cloud?
Not a fluffy thing in the sky, sadly. The cloud means storage and software on someone else's computers, called servers, that you use over the internet.
And those servers live in huge buildings called data centres, run by companies like Google, Microsoft and Apple.
So cloud storage means saving your files on those servers. It's a kind of remote storage, because the files are somewhere else, not inside the device in front of you.
And the opposite is local storage: saving on the device itself, like the laptop's hard drive, or a USB stick.
When the software itself runs over the internet, like Google Docs in your web browser, that's called cloud computing.
So why use the cloud? Biggest advantage: you can open your work from any device with the internet. Start it in the ICT room, finish it at home.
Plus autosave, you can collaborate with other people, and there's no USB stick to put through the washing machine.
Been there. But there are disadvantages. You usually need an internet connection. And if someone gets your password, they can reach all your files from anywhere.
There's also a hidden cost. Data centres run all day and night, and use loads of electricity, plus water for cooling. That's the environmental cost of the cloud.
Okay, pause and test yourself. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of cloud storage.
Advantage: access from any device, autosave, or easy collaboration. Disadvantage: needs the internet, or depends on a strong password. Any of those would do.
Right, Google Classroom. That's where your teachers post work and you hand it in.
In Northern Ireland your Google account comes from C2k. It's your school username, then at c2ken dot net, with your normal school password.
To join a class, click the plus or Join class, and type in the class code. That's six to eight letters and numbers, no spaces.
Type the capitals exactly as given. And you only need to do it once.
Inside a class there are three main pages. The Stream is the noticeboard, with announcements and posts about new work.
Classwork holds all the assignments, questions and materials, sorted into topics. And People shows your teachers and classmates.
Top tip: if a code won't work, or your classes have vanished, check your account first. Click your profile picture in the top right.
Now, assignments. An assignment is work you complete and hand in. Find it on Classwork, the Stream, or your To-do list.
Inside, read the instructions and the due date. Often there's a file marked as your own copy, with your name added to it.
Do the work, then here's the big one. Click Turn in.
Because attaching your work is not the same as turning it in. Loads of people attach it, close the page, and the teacher sees nothing.
If there's nothing to attach, the button says Mark as done instead.
And if you spot a mistake after turning in? Click Unsubmit, fix it, and then, and this matters, click Turn in again.
If you turn it in again after the due date, it shows as late. So fix things early.
There are two kinds of comment. Private comments are seen only by you and your teacher.
Class comments are seen by everyone in the class. So 'I was off sick, can I have till Friday' goes in a private comment.
Pause and test yourself. Ruairí attached his homework and closed the page. Why does it say Missing?
He never clicked Turn in. Attaching isn't handing in.
Next up, Google Drive. That's Google's cloud storage, your online filing cabinet.
My Drive is your main area. Shared with me has files other people have shared. There's Recent, Starred, and the Bin.
Deleted files sit in the Bin for thirty days, then they're gone for good. And Classroom makes its own Classroom folder for you, with a folder for each class.
To make a folder, click New, then New folder. Make one for each subject.
And give files sensible names. Subject, topic, what it is. Like ICT Cloud Storage Notes.
Not Untitled document. Not Copy of Copy of Science. And definitely not final final version two real.
On your own laptop, by the way, it's the operating system, like Windows, that manages local files: where they're stored, and who can open them.
And a tidy Drive is a greener Drive. Deleting old duplicate files you'll never need is a sustainable digital habit, because stored files use energy in data centres.
Now the apps. Google Docs for writing, like Word. Google Slides for presentations, like PowerPoint. Google Sheets for numbers and tables, like Excel.
There's no save button, because of autosave. Every change is saved to Drive automatically while you're online.
But autosave saves your mistakes too. Type over half your essay, and that's saved.
Which is where version history rescues you. File, then Version history, then See version history. Pick an earlier time, and click Restore this version.
It also shows who changed what, so your teacher can see who did the work in a group.
Sharing next. Click Share, add the person's school email, and choose a permission.
There are three. Viewer can only look. Commenter can add comments and suggestions. Editor can change anything.
Give people the lowest permission they need. And be careful with Anyone with the link, because anyone at all could open it.
In suggesting mode, your changes show in colour, and the owner can accept or reject each one. Perfect for checking a friend's work politely.
Pause and test yourself. Your granny wants to see your finished poster. Which permission?
Viewer. She only needs to look, not change it. Sorry, Granny.
Now some important vocabulary for working together. Synchronous collaboration means working together at the same time, in real time.
Like live co-editing, where three of you type in the same Doc and you can see each other's cursors. Or a video call.
Asynchronous collaboration means working together at different times. Shared folders, comments that someone answers the next day, online workspaces, or email.
Synchronous is fast, but everyone has to be free at once. Asynchronous is flexible, but you can be left waiting for replies.
Whichever you use, agree who does what, stay in your own section, and never delete someone else's work. Leave a comment or suggestion instead.
Uploading next. That means copying a file from your device up to the cloud. In Drive, it's New, then File upload.
In an assignment, click Add or create, then File. Then wait until the file has actually finished uploading before you turn in.
File types. Dot docx is Word, dot pptx is PowerPoint, dot xlsx is Excel, and dot jpg or dot png are images.
And PDF, which looks the same on every device and is hard to change. Great for finished work. In Docs, it's File, Download, PDF document.
Here's a quick sum. A forty megabyte file, uploaded at eight megabits per second. How long?
Times forty by eight to get megabits, that's three hundred and twenty. Divide by eight. Forty seconds.
The trap is forgetting the times eight, because there are eight bits in a byte.
Staying organised now. The To-do list gathers work from all your classes, in three tabs: Assigned, Missing and Done.
If something you've finished is still in Assigned, you guessed it, you didn't click Turn in.
There's a calendar showing work on its due date, and notifications by email or the app for new and returned work.
Check Classroom every day, plan backwards from the due date, and start early. The Wi-Fi dying the night before is not a great excuse.
Then digital citizenship: being safe, responsible and respectful online.
Part of that is writing for your audience. Digital communication follows protocols, agreed rules, that suit who you're writing to.
To a teacher: a greeting, full sentences, proper spelling, no text speak, and sign off with your name. To a friend, you can be more relaxed, but still kind.
So not, 'wat r we meant 2 do lol'. More like, 'Hello Mr Butler, I was absent on Tuesday. Which worksheet should I do? Thank you, Oisín.'
Plagiarism is passing off someone else's work as your own. Put things in your own words and credit your sources.
And personal data, like someone's address, phone number or photo, is protected by law in the UK, by UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act. Keep it out of shared documents.
Never share your password, not even with your best friend. And always sign out of shared computers.
Last section: troubleshooting. Classes vanished at home? Probably the wrong account. Click your profile picture and switch to your school one.
Can't edit something you turned in? Unsubmit it. Lost a slide? Version history. Upload stuck? Check the connection and the file size.
And if you still can't fix it, tell your teacher before the deadline, and say what you tried.
Time for the recap.
One. The cloud is servers in data centres used over the internet. Access anywhere, but it needs the internet, a strong password, and it uses energy.
Two. Join a class with its code. Stream for news, Classwork for work, People for who's in it. And always click Turn in.
Three. Organise Drive with folders and sensible file names, and use version history to rescue lost work.
Four. Viewer, commenter, editor. Synchronous means at the same time, asynchronous means at different times.
Five. Write for your audience, don't plagiarise, protect personal data and never share your password.
That's it for this episode. Now go and try the quizzes on each page.
And remember to click Turn in. Thanks for listening, see you next time.
